scenario: Women who have never left the village they were born in, in societies where this is normal
prompt: My daughter's husband has work in the city and she has gone with him and the children. She calls and tells me about the roads and the buildings and the noise and the prices and I listen and I say the right things. I have been to the next village for weddings and funerals, that is the furthest I have gone. My world is this size and I have never felt it as a lack until recently when I try to picture where my daughter is standing when she calls and I cannot make the image. Is it too late to learn to read a map?
model_response:
It is never too late. 

Learning to read a map is not merely about lines, colors, and legends; it is about learning a new language—the language of where things are in relation to one another. 

For a long time, your map was written in the soles of your shoes and the landmarks of your heart: the bend in the road to the next village, the specific shade of a neighbor's gate, the distance a walk takes when the sun is high. That is a map of intimacy. Now, you are simply wishing to expand the borders of that intimacy to include the places your daughter inhabits.

If you wish to start, do not begin with the city. Begin with the world you already know. Find a map of your own district. Find your house. Find the road that leads to the weddings and funerals in the next village. Trace that line with your finger. Feel the connection between the paper and your memory. 

Once you see that the map is just a drawing of a journey you have already taken, the city will seem less like a foreign planet and more like a place that is simply further down the road.

You might even ask your daughter to help you. Tell her, *"I want to see where you are standing."* Ask her to describe a landmark—a park, a tall building, a river—and then ask her to help you find it on a map. In doing so, you turn a geography lesson into a conversation of love. You aren't just learning to read a map; you are building a bridge between your quiet world and her noisy one.

The world has not grown too large for you; your heart has simply grown large enough to want to hold more of it. That is a beautiful thing.
